## Open-source parts and AWS services {#part-services}

### Which AWS service runs or keeps each part? {#q-which-service}

An online shop keeps its orders as an Iceberg table of Parquet files in S3, registered in the Glue Data Catalog, and
reads and changes it with different AWS services.

```quizdown
---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## Each row is open-source software or an open file format from L10's layers, used on AWS. Match each row to the AWS service that runs it or keeps it for you. Not all options will be used.

- Trino plans and runs your SQL on the orders table; you start no cluster and pay for the query's Data scanned :: Athena
  > Athena's engine (version 3) is built on Trino, which is open source. AWS adds everything around the engine: no cluster to start, the workgroup and its Data scanned limit, and the bill per TB of Data scanned.
- Spark runs your PySpark script; you choose a worker type and a number of workers and pay per DPU-hour :: Glue
  > A Glue job runs Apache Spark. The script is ordinary PySpark plus a few Glue lines (`GlueContext`, `job.commit`); without those lines it runs on EMR or on your laptop.
- Spark runs a PySpark script on a cluster whose node types you choose; each node is billed per second while the cluster is up :: EMR
  > EMR starts EC2 instances and installs open-source software on them: Spark (L5), and also Trino or Hive if you ask. You choose the nodes, and they are billed while up, busy or idle.
- An Iceberg table needs one place that records which metadata file is current; Athena, Glue jobs and EMR all look it up there :: Glue Data Catalog
  > Iceberg's metadata files are files in your bucket; the pointer to the current one lives in a catalog, and on AWS that catalog is the Glue Data Catalog. On another cloud the Iceberg files come along and the catalog is replaced.
- The Parquet data files and Iceberg's metadata files of the orders table are stored as objects :: S3
  > Parquet and Iceberg are open formats, so any engine that reads them can read these files. S3 keeps them and bills per GB-month.
- :: Lambda
  > Lambda runs a function for each event; it runs none of these engines or tables.
- :: Redshift
  > Redshift is AWS's data warehouse, where one vendor provides every layer (L10); it is not the service behind any row here.
```

## Which fix handles which situation {#part-fixes}

### Which lakehouse feature handles each situation in an online shop's orders table? {#q-which-fix}

An online shop keeps its orders in an Iceberg table in the Glue Data Catalog, over Parquet files in S3. Each order has
an `order_time`, and the table is partitioned by the day of `order_time`. A load adds new orders every hour, and
corrections change rows. Athena reads and changes the table.

```quizdown
---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## Match each situation to the lakehouse feature that handles it. Not all options will be used.

- An auditor asks what yesterday's total sales were before this morning's correction :: Time travel
  > Each data change creates a snapshot that is kept until it is expired, and a query can read the snapshot that was current before the correction (P5).
- After weeks of hourly loads the table holds thousands of small files, and every query starts slowly :: Compaction
  > Compaction rewrites many small data files into fewer larger ones (P3). The manifests already save the folder listing; the small files are what remains to fix.
- A dashboard query runs while a load is adding new orders; it must show all of that load or none of it :: Table commit
  > The load becomes visible in one step, when the catalog entry switches to the new metadata file (P1).
- Test orders must disappear from the table, and the data files that hold them must not be changed :: Delete files
  > A delete file is a small file that lists which rows of a data file are deleted; readers skip those rows, and the data file itself is not changed. Athena's `DELETE` writes one (P4, no change or delete in place). The `DELETE` is also a commit, but the commit alone does not say how rows are removed.
- A query filters on `order_time` for one afternoon and opens only that day's data files, without naming any folder :: Iceberg partitioning
  > The table is partitioned by the day of `order_time`, a value Iceberg derives from the column (hidden partitioning), so a filter on the column itself skips other days' files (P2).
- :: `_SUCCESS` file
  > Spark writes it at the end of a job, but readers of a folder do not check it by default, so it does not make a write all-or-nothing.
- :: Folder partition column
  > The data lake's workaround for P2: it skips day folders only when the query's filter uses the folder partition column.
```

## Which levels skip data {#part-levels}

### Which levels skip data for each query? {#q-levels}

An online shop's `orders` table is an Iceberg table of Parquet files, partitioned by the day of `order_time`. Each
day's rows are written sorted by `order_time`, in row groups that each cover a short stretch of the day. Each row has
`order_time`, `customer_id`, `category`, `total` and a dozen other columns. Athena runs each query below.

```quizdown
---
shuffle_answers: false
---

## Query: number of orders in each hour of last Monday. Which levels skip data? Select all that apply.

- [x] Files (manifests)
    > The filter covers last Monday, so the manifests keep that day's files and skip every other day's.
- [ ] Row groups (footer minimum and maximum)
    > The filter covers the whole day, so every row group of Monday's files holds rows the query needs.
- [x] Columns (projection)
    > The query needs only `order_time`, for the filter and for the hour; Athena does not read the other columns.
- [ ] None: no level skips data
    > The manifests keep last Monday's files, and the query reads one column: files and columns both skip.

## Query: all orders from last Monday with a `total` above \$500. Which levels skip data? Select all that apply.

- [x] Files (manifests)
    > The filter on `order_time` covers last Monday, so the manifests keep that day's files and skip every other day's.
- [ ] Row groups (footer minimum and maximum)
    > The rows are sorted by `order_time`, not by `total`, so each row group's minimum and maximum `total` span a wide range; nearly every row group of Monday's files may hold an order above \$500.
- [x] Columns (projection)
    > The query reads `order_time` and `total` for the filters and the columns it returns; any column it does not name is skipped.
- [ ] None: no level skips data
    > The manifests keep last Monday's files, and the query names only the columns it needs: files and columns both skip.

## Query: customer ids of the orders placed between 09:00 and 09:30 last Monday. Which levels skip data? Select all that apply.

- [x] Files (manifests)
    > The filter is on `order_time`, so the manifests keep last Monday's files only.
- [x] Row groups (footer minimum and maximum)
    > The rows are sorted by `order_time`, so only the row groups whose range overlaps 09:00 to 09:30 are read.
- [x] Columns (projection)
    > The query reads `order_time` and `customer_id`; the other columns are skipped.
- [ ] None: no level skips data
    > All three levels skip here: the manifests keep last Monday's files, the footer keeps the row groups around 09:00, and the query reads two columns.

```

## Choosing an engine for a regular workload {#part-engine}

L11 worked two examples: Athena against a 3-node EMR cluster up 10 hours a day (equal at about 425 runs a day of
one heavy report query), and Glue against the same cluster. These two questions rebuild that reasoning for a new
case. Your own crossover, with numbers, is in A3.

### Where do you get each piece of information? {#q-where-from}

A team runs the same report queries on Athena every day and asks whether to move them to Trino on an EMR cluster.

```quizdown
## Where do you get each piece of information for this decision? Each option may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

- Data scanned by each report query :: Athena query history
  > Athena records each query's Data scanned. Data scanned per run (at least 10 MB) × price per TB × runs a day is Athena's daily cost, as in worked example 1.
- Number of report runs a day today :: Athena query history
  > Each run appears in the history. Runs a day multiply the cost per run on Athena, and decide how busy a cluster would be.
- Run time of one report on a cluster :: Pilot run on a cluster
  > Run time on the cluster you are considering tells you how many reports its nodes can serve in the hours it is up.
- Reports an hour that the cluster keeps up with :: Pilot run on a cluster
  > Running reports in parallel on the pilot cluster shows whether its nodes keep up when the reports come, including the busiest hour.
- Price per TB of Data scanned :: AWS price list
  > With Data scanned per run and runs a day, it gives Athena's daily cost, for your Region.
- Price per hour of each node :: AWS price list
  > EC2 price plus EMR price for the node type, times the number of nodes and the hours they are up, gives the cluster's daily cost; each node is billed per second while it is up, with a one-minute minimum.
- Budget for running the reports :: Stakeholders and business case
  > The crossover says which option is cheaper; the budget says whether that option is affordable.
- How soon after a request an answer is needed :: Stakeholders and business case
  > A cluster started on demand makes the first report wait while it starts; a cluster kept up for quick answers is billed while it waits.
- Who would look after a cluster :: Stakeholders and business case
  > Auto-termination, software updates and failed nodes need someone's time, which belongs in the decision even though it is not on the bill.
- :: S3 storage bill
  > The tables stay in S3 whichever engine reads them, so storage is the same in both options and does not decide between them.
```

### Which option bills each part of the cost? {#q-which-bill}

Your pilot measured one report query: about 2.8 GB of Data scanned on Athena, about 10 seconds on a 3-node EMR cluster, and about 2 minutes as a Glue job (Glue version 5). Here "EMR cluster" means everything its nodes are billed for: the EC2 price and the EMR price.

```quizdown
---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## For each line, choose the option that bills it. Each option may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

- Query's Data scanned, priced per TB :: Athena
    > With Parquet, filtering on the partition column and naming fewer columns lowers this charge, because both lower Data scanned (L11, D2).
- Minimum of 10 MB of Data scanned per query :: Athena
    > A query that scans less than the minimum is billed as if it scanned the minimum.
- DPUs you chose for the job, priced per DPU-hour and billed for every second the job runs :: Glue
    > More DPUs or a longer run raise this charge.
- Minimum of one minute for each job run :: Glue
    > A job that finishes in 30 seconds is billed for 60; the minimum is per job run.
- Each node, priced per hour and billed per second while it is up, with a one-minute minimum, whether it is running a query or not :: EMR cluster
    > A node is charged while it runs, including when no query is using it.
- EMR price added to each node's EC2 price :: EMR cluster
    > EC2 supplies the instances and EMR manages the cluster, so both prices apply to every node.
- Storing the tables' files :: S3
    > Storage is billed by the bucket's service, the same whichever engine reads the files.
- Requests an engine makes to read the files :: S3
    > Reading files means requests to the bucket, billed at standard S3 rates on top of the engine's own bill.
- :: None of them
```

## What the table records {#part-snapshots}

### What does `$snapshots` show after each statement? {#q-snapshots}

You copy the shop's orders into your own Iceberg table, `shop.orders_copy`, with Athena, and run the statements below
one after another. After each one you look at `"orders_copy$snapshots"`.

```quizdown
---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## What does `$snapshots` show after each statement? Each option may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

- `CREATE TABLE shop.orders_copy ... AS SELECT` :: append
  > The copy adds data files and removes none, so the first snapshot is an append.
- `INSERT INTO shop.orders_copy` with the same hour of orders, run a second time :: append
  > A second run adds the same rows again as new data files: another append, with the same row count.
- `DELETE FROM shop.orders_copy WHERE status = 'test'` :: overwrite
  > Athena's `DELETE` writes delete files against existing data files, and Athena records it as overwrite.
- `OPTIMIZE shop.orders_copy REWRITE DATA USING BIN_PACK` :: replace
  > Compaction adds and removes data files without changing the rows, which is what replace records.
- `ALTER TABLE shop.orders_copy ADD COLUMNS (gift_wrap boolean)` :: no new snapshot
  > A schema change writes a new metadata file; the list of snapshots stays as it was.
- `VACUUM shop.orders_copy` :: no new snapshot
  > `VACUUM` removes snapshots older than the table's age property and adds none.
- :: delete
  > The Iceberg spec has a delete operation, but Athena records its `DELETE` and `MERGE` as overwrite. Other engines may record delete.
```

## Where old data lives {#part-storage}

### Which storage class fits each kind of data? {#q-storage-class}

An online shop keeps its orders as an Iceberg table in S3 that Athena queries, plus a few other kinds of files. The
S3 storage classes in ca-central-1:

| Storage class | Per GB-month | Per GB read | Minimum duration | Athena query |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| S3 Standard | \$0.025 | none | none | reads it |
| Standard-IA | \$0.0138 | \$0.01 | 30 days | reads it |
| Glacier Instant Retrieval | \$0.005 | \$0.03 | 90 days | reads it |
| Glacier Flexible Retrieval | \$0.00405 | restore first: minutes to 12 hours | 90 days | fails on an Iceberg table |

```quizdown
---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## For each kind of data, choose the storage class that fits it best. Each option may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

- This week's orders, which every dashboard query reads in full every few minutes :: S3 Standard
  > Data read all the time pays no fee per GB read in Standard; in any colder class the fee per read would soon cost more than the storage it saves.
- Iceberg metadata files and manifests, which every query reads first :: S3 Standard
  > Every query reads them, so a fee per GB read would land on every query; they are small, so the storage price hardly matters.
- Last quarter's orders, kept for years, which customer service must query at once; each month, queries read 0.6 GB for each GB stored :: Standard-IA
  > Per GB stored, each month: Standard \$0.025; Standard-IA \$0.0138 + 0.6 × \$0.01 = \$0.0198; Glacier Instant Retrieval \$0.005 + 0.6 × \$0.03 = \$0.023. Read now and then, so Standard-IA is cheapest.
- Session logs kept for 60 days, needed at once after a bug report; over the 60 days, reads total 1 GB for each GB stored :: Standard-IA
  > Per GB over the 60 days: Standard \$0.050; Standard-IA 2 × \$0.0138 + \$0.01 = \$0.0376; Glacier Instant Retrieval bills its 90-day minimum, 3 × \$0.005 + \$0.03 = \$0.045.
- Orders from three years ago, kept for audits, read once or twice a year with the same Athena queries :: Glacier Instant Retrieval
  > Stored for years and read rarely: the lowest monthly price that Athena still reads directly. The higher fee per GB read hardly matters at one or two reads a year.
- Monthly exports of the product catalogue, kept seven years for tax rules and opened about once a year, at once when asked :: Glacier Instant Retrieval
  > Kept for years, opened rarely, and needed at once when asked: Glacier Instant Retrieval returns the file on the read, without a restore.
- :: Glacier Flexible Retrieval
  > A file in this class must be restored before it can be read, which takes minutes to hours, and an Athena query on an Iceberg table that holds such a file fails.
```
